name: Hot-cloth makeup removal

lead: Hot-cloth cleansing means pressing a warm, damp washcloth onto the face to loosen makeup that has been broken down with an oil or balm cleanser, then wiping it away. It is popular in double-cleansing routines.

The appearance payoff comes from clean skin: removing heavy makeup and sunscreen thoroughly leaves a clear base for skincare, and facialists and makeup artists also describe a light polishing effect that smooths the surface for concealer.

paras: Users usually massage a cleansing balm or oil over dry skin, then hold or wipe with a warm, soft cloth and rinse, sometimes following with a second water-based cleanser. A clean cloth is typically used each time.
Very hot water can irritate or redden skin, and reused cloths can carry bacteria. Rubbing hard around the eyes may cause irritation.

Warm cloth lifts it away and polishes the surface
Clean, smooth base for skincare and makeup
angle.text: Users employ the method to take off heavy makeup gently, without scrubbing, and to leave skin clean and smooth for the rest of a routine and for the next day's makeup.

lead: Hot-cloth cleansing is a method in which a warm, damp cloth is used with an oil or balm cleanser to dissolve and wipe off makeup and leftover product. It is a common step in double-cleansing routines, especially for heavy or waterproof makeup and water-resistant sunscreen.[1][2]

People use it to leave the skin clean and slightly polished: beauty editors and professionals describe the cloth as removing residue that water alone can leave behind, giving mild exfoliation and a smoother surface for concealer and skincare.[3][4] Dermatologists quoted in consumer coverage recommend a gentle oil or balm cleanse followed by a mild water-based cleanser as more thorough than makeup wipes.[2]
infobox: Soft washcloth or muslin cloth, warm water, cleansing balm or oil
Clean cloth each time, washed after use[4]

paras: Cleansing oils and balms are lipid-soluble cleansers used in double cleansing, a routine for residues that resist a single wash: the product is worked over dry skin for a set time, then a water-based cleanser is applied and the face is rinsed.[1] The hot-cloth step replaces or follows the rinse, with a damp cloth used to remove the oil and the dissolved makeup.[3][4]

Cult Beauty's guide describes the cloth as using steam and gentle friction to help loosen residue, with the cloth soaked in hot water, wrung out and laid over the face a couple of times, then rinsed in lukewarm water and used in small circles to polish the skin.[3]

Descriptions in beauty coverage follow a common pattern: remove eye and face makeup, massage an oil or balm over dry skin and emulsify with warm water, follow with a cream or second cleanser if desired, then hold a hot damp cloth over the face and wipe away residue before applying serum or moisturiser.[3] Makeup artist Katie Jane Hughes recommends a cloth at night for its light conditioning and exfoliating effect, and facialist Ashleigh Scott says a hot cloth removes oil-based cleanser better than rinsing with water alone.[4]
Users generally use a clean cloth for each cleanse and wash the cloths after use; one writer describes rotating six muslin cloths.[4]

Proponents cite removal of leftover cleanser and makeup, gentle physical exfoliation, less pore congestion, better absorption of serums and moisturisers, and stimulation of circulation from the massage.[3][4] These are descriptions from beauty editors, facialists and makeup artists rather than measured outcomes.

Beauty guides say the water should be hot but not too hot and advise avoiding dragging the skin, especially around the eyes where skin is less elastic.[3] A dermatologist quoted about oil cleansers advises warm rather than hot water because very hot water can strip the skin barrier.

Dermatologist Lauren Ploch, speaking about reusable cleansing cloths, describes them as generally safe when used appropriately, advises one or two gentle passes per area because more scrubbing can cause irritation and thickening of the outer skin layer, and notes cloths become coarser with repeated use; people with sensitive skin or rosacea are advised to take particular care.[5]
